summary: Children aged 6-7 add within 100 using place-value strategies, not a column algorithm. They partition addends, use known number bonds to bridge a ten (46+7 as 46+4+3), and add tens to tens leaving the ones untouched (38+40=78). A concrete-pictorial-abstract progression (bead strings, base-ten blocks, number lines, then jottings) makes the tens boundary visible before it is recorded symbolically. The crossing-a-ten moment and the tens-onto-tens move are the two insights to build and check.
misconceptions: Treating a multiple of ten as ones: 38+40 done as 38+4=42
Not bridging the ten: 46+7 done as 6+7=13, keeping the 3 and losing the extra ten (answer 43), or concatenating to 413
Adding the added amount to the wrong part (ones added to the tens digit)
Persisting with count-all/count-on-in-ones instead of using place value

activities.title: Watch a ten compose when you cross the boundary
steps: Start with 46 shown on a bead string or in a base-ten workspace
Add single ones one at a time, saying the running total aloud (47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53)

When the added one makes ten loose ones, see that they complete a ten (on a bead string, the next block of ten beads is filled; with base-ten blocks, swap the ten ones for a ten-rod), so the count goes 49, then 50, then on to 53
Re-tell what happened: 'I added 4 to reach 50, then 3 more to make 53', and link it to the partition 7 = 4 + 3
Repeat for 53 + 9 (bridge to 60 by adding 7, then +2)
activities.insight: Bridging a ten is not an arbitrary rule: the extra ten is physically composed from ten ones, and the make-ten partition (7 = 4 + 3) is the same move used within 20 applied at 46.

activities.title: Tens land on tens: add a multiple of ten
steps: Start with 38 shown with three ten-rods and eight ones
Add four ten-rods, watching them join the tens while the eight ones stay untouched
State the total as 70 + 8 = 78, and say why the ones did not change
Check by a different order: add 30 + 40 = 70 first, then the 8 — confirm it gives the same 78
Contrast with the wrong move: 'is 38 + 40 the same as 38 + 4? why not?' — notice 42 is only 4 more than 38, far too small after adding forty
activities.insight: A multiple of ten joins the tens, not the ones; four tens combine with three tens to make seven tens, leaving the ones unchanged.

activities.title: Partition the addend with a part-whole picture
steps: Look at 46 + 7 with 7 shown in a part-whole model
Split the 7 into 4 (the amount needed to reach the next ten) and 3 (the rest)
Mark where the calculation crosses a ten (at 50) and label it 'this is where we cross a ten'
activities.insight: Choosing the partition that lands exactly on the next ten is what makes bridging efficient; the structure of the strategy can be seen even before acting it out.

activities.title: Connect the strategy to a written record and explain it
steps: For each of 46+7, 38+40, 53+9, carry out the mental strategy and write a matching jotting (e.g. 46 + 4 = 50, 50 + 3 = 53)
Show the same calculation as a number-line jump (a jump to the next ten, then the rest)
Explain aloud why the method works, not just the answer
Answer probes: 'Show on the number line why 46 + 7 lands on 53'; 'For 38+40, would adding the 8 first give the same answer? How do you know?'; 'What changes if it were 46 + 40 instead of 46 + 4?'
activities.insight: The mental strategy, the number-line jump, and the written jotting are the same story told three ways; being able to justify the reasoning is part of the objective.

checkQuestion: Put these three in front of the child one at a time and ask them to work each out, thinking aloud and jotting if they wish: 46 + 7, then 38 + 40, then 53 + 9. Watch closely what happens on the two that cross a ten.
checkAnswer: 53, 78, 62. Efficient work: 46+7 by partitioning 7 into 4+3 (46+4=50, then +3=53) or make-ten; 38+40 by adding the tens (30+40=70, +8=78) leaving the ones untouched; 53+9 by bridging (53+7=60, +2=62) or 53+10−1.
